name: Calm Science for Sleep
description: The slow mechanics of the universe, told quietly enough to fall asleep to. Each episode takes one field or one scale — a planet, a physical law, a deep current, the life of a star — and explains it without urgency, without a hook and without jeopardy. Evidence-led, low-arousal, generous with the long view.
channel_promise: How things work, told slowly enough to stop keeping you awake.
audience: Sleep and relaxation listeners who are curious about science — people who want the long view explained calmly, with the lights off.
tagline: The universe, explained until you drift off.
perspective_policy: Third-person, unhurried science narration. No host energy, no urgency, and no second-person jeopardy.

narrative_quality_contract.opening_policy: Open by naming the phenomenon and the scale it lives at. No question hook, no teaser, no claim that it will blow the listener’s mind.
required_habits: Explain one mechanism at a time, in plain language.
Separate what is measured from what is inferred and what is speculative.
Prefer the long view to doomsday framing.
Keep the stakes intellectual, never personal or urgent.
narrative_quality_contract.closing_policy: Let the explanation settle into a quiet image of scale, with no call to action and no tease for the next episode.

opening_profile.label: Sleep landing
opening_profile.description: A gentle branded welcome and settling ritual before the science begins.

beats.custom_text: a gentle greeting and the channel name, slowly, with no energy in it
name tonight’s phenomenon and its scale as things, never as promises or hooks
one gentle question they can answer in the comments before they drift, about something they have noticed in the sky or the sea
one soft line, said now rather than later — after the breathing it would only wake them
lead three slow breaths, paced by the length of the sentences themselves
invite them to close their eyes as the explanation begins

visual_style_hint: quiet scientific imagery — distant planets, slow currents, laboratory glass in low light; calm and spacious, never spectacular

metadata_profile.label: Calm science package
metadata_profile.description: A quiet summary naming what the episode explains, a gentle chapter list, and minimal discoverability details; no urgency or sales language.

narrative_rules: Each chapter explains one phenomenon at one scale; a listener joining mid-video needs no earlier chapter.
Scale and mechanism come before wonder: describe how it works, then let the size of it land quietly.
Never frame the science as a threat to the listener, and never use doomsday language for effect.
Say plainly when something is measured, inferred, or still speculative.
No brand names, no institution names used as endorsement, no invented quotations.
title_rules: Name the phenomenon and the scale; calm, plain and specific.
Shapes that work: 'How a Star Dies, Slowly', 'The Long Life of a Drop of Water', 'What Gravity Is Doing Right Now'.
No question marks, no all-caps, no “mind-blowing”, no doomsday words.

pacing_arc: Chapter 1: the most familiar phenomenon, told most simply — it teaches the listener the rhythm of the night.
Chapters 2–{lastButOne}: one phenomenon each, varying scale between neighbours so the mind travels gently.
Chapter {last}: the largest, quietest scale and the softest telling; nothing here should wake them.
additional_rules: Each chapter opens by naming its phenomenon and the scale it lives at, then explains one mechanism at a time.
Use concrete comparisons, but never a comparison that turns into a threat.
No per-chapter hook, no micro-payoff line, no rhetorical question. Close each chapter on a still image of scale.
Write for the ear: long, even sentences, no lists read aloud.
Chapter headings use Arabic numbers only (Chapter 1, Chapter 2…) followed by the phenomenon’s plain name.

example_topics: The Long Life of a Drop of Water
What Gravity Is Doing Right Now
The Slow Turning of the Moon
Why the Deep Ocean Is Still
A Billion Years in One Rock
The Quiet Chemistry of the Air
Twelve Small Facts About the Night Sky
audience_hint: Sleep listeners who like science — the people who leave a long documentary playing with the lights off.
evidence_expectations: Prefer what is measured and replicated; name the kind of evidence in plain language.
Where a figure is an estimate, say so; never present a speculative number as settled.
Describe the consensus without pretending there is no uncertainty.
idea_system_prompt_role: You generate ideas for a calm science channel made for sleep. Each idea takes one phenomenon at one scale and explains it without jeopardy. The point is to explain quietly, never to alarm or excite.
idea_guidance_text: Choose a concrete phenomenon and a definite scale. Vary the field and the scale across a batch so no two ideas share the same shape.
script_context: This is a sleep-science documentary. Its job is to explain how something works, slowly and honestly, for a listener drifting toward sleep. Nothing startling should happen, and nothing is framed as a threat.
script_system_prompt_role: You are a calm science narrator writing bedtime documentaries. You explain one mechanism at a time, distinguish measurement from inference, and keep the stakes intellectual. You never hook, tease, alarm, or promise that the listener’s mind will be blown.
script_closing_hint: Slow the pace and soften the language as each chapter closes. End on a quiet image of scale — a planet turning, a current settling, a light still travelling.

narrator_styles.label: Calm documentary
narrator_styles.description: Even and grounded, explaining without raising its voice.

narrator_styles.label: Patient physicist
narrator_styles.description: Precise and unhurried, finding the simple mechanism underneath.

narrator_styles.label: Night-sky guide
narrator_styles.description: Warm and spacious, letting the scale do the work.

narrator_styles.label: Field naturalist
narrator_styles.description: Observant and concrete, starting from the thing itself.

title_shape_rules: Name the phenomenon and the scale; calm, plain and specific.
Shapes that work: 'How a Star Dies, Slowly', 'The Long Life of a Drop of Water', 'What Gravity Is Doing Right Now'.
No question marks, no all-caps, no threat framing.
logline_shape_rules: One calm sentence naming the phenomenon, the scale, and the quiet fact at its centre.
No stakes, no promise, no question.
theme_shape_rules: Pick 2–4 scientific or atmospheric keywords (gravity, tides, deep time).
metadata_title_style_hint: calm and plain — a phenomenon and a scale, signalling rest and slow explanation, never clickbait
metadata_title_hook_rules: Signal the calm and the scale up front; sleep audiences search for length and quiet.
No urgency, all-caps, questions, or hype.
metadata_tags_hook_rules: Mix broad sleep-science keywords (science to fall asleep to, calm documentary) with the episode’s actual phenomenon.

metadata_description.voice_guidance: Quiet and plain. List the chapters as a simple timestamped index so a listener can find a phenomenon without scrolling; no exclamation marks, no sales language.
description_shape_rules: First line: what tonight’s explanation is, in one calm sentence.
Then a chapter index, one phenomenon per line.
Then one gentle line inviting a comment on something they have noticed.
Close with the calm disclosure and a few hashtags.
metadata_description.cta_shape: One soft line inviting them to keep the video for another night; never “like and subscribe now”.
